h1: Noida offices, American buyers: SEO across time zones
metaTitle: SEO Company in Noida for US and EU Buyer Search
metaDescription: Most Noida IT and edtech firms sell abroad. Here's how to rank inside US and EU results from an Indian address, priced in INR, on a 90-day guarantee.
answer: Most Noida IT-services and edtech companies sell to buyers who will never type the word Noida. That makes the job international SEO, not local SEO: hreflang set correctly, a domain that doesn't shout India, a link profile that isn't all `.in`, and Search Console filtered to the country you actually sell to.
takeaways: If your revenue is in dollars, ranking #1 for "software company in Noida" is worth almost nothing. Your buyer isn't searching for a city.
A `.in` domain carries an India signal you can no longer override — Google retired the country-targeting control in Search Console.
Unfiltered Search Console will show you an India-heavy impression profile and make you think nothing's working. Filter by country before you judge anything.
Edtech admission queries and IT-services RFP queries need completely different pages, cadences and seasonal planning.
A big share of your local Noida search demand is job seekers, not buyers. Optimising for it produces a careers-page traffic chart and no pipeline.

sections.h2: Your buyer will never type the word Noida
body: Noida's economy runs on export. IT and IT-enabled services along the Sector 62 corridor, edtech and media down the Expressway, engineering teams serving clients in the US, UK, Germany and the Gulf. The invoices are in dollars, euros and pounds.

Which makes most SEO proposals sent to Noida companies structurally wrong. They arrive optimised for "IT company in Noida" and "best software development company Noida" — queries typed by candidates, vendors and competitors doing research. A procurement manager in Ohio hunting an offshore engineering partner types none of them.
The job is international SEO run from an Indian address: a different technical brief, a different content brief, a different measurement setup, and almost none of it about your city.

callout.title: Check this before you spend anything
callout.body: Open Search Console, go to the performance report, and filter Country to the market you actually sell to. If that filter removes 90% of your impressions, every optimisation you've paid for so far has been aimed at the wrong hemisphere.

sections.h2: The technical setup for ranking in US and EU results
body: There are four decisions here, and companies usually get the cheap ones right and the expensive one wrong.

subs.h3: Domain: this is the one that's hard to undo
body: A `.in` domain carries a country signal, and Google retired the country-targeting control in Search Console, so no setting left says "actually, we sell to America". A generic top-level domain — `.com`, `.io`, `.co` — is geographically neutral.

If you're already on `.in` with years of equity, don't panic-migrate. A migration risks the traffic you have, and a strong `.com` you don't own yet may cost more than a quarter of retainer. But if you're choosing today, choose the neutral one.

subs.h3: Hreflang: a swap instruction, not a ranking boost
body: If you run more than one regional version — `/us/`, `/uk/`, `/in/` — hreflang tells Google which to serve which searcher. It must be reciprocal: every page points at every equivalent, including itself, plus an `x-default`.
It doesn't make you rank. It stops the wrong version ranking. Teams who install it expecting the first outcome conclude it doesn't work.

subs.h3: Hosting: mostly a red herring, with one real edge
body: Server location is a weak signal and a CDN makes it weaker. Where it genuinely matters is speed: a US buyer hitting an origin in Noida with no edge caching feels every millisecond, and Core Web Vitals are measured from where the user is, not where you are.

subs.h3: Links: the part that actually decides it
body: If every referring domain you have is a `.in` directory or an Indian news site, you look like an Indian business to a search engine, because you are. Ranking for a US commercial query usually needs coverage on domains that a US buyer's results already contain.
This is the slow, expensive half of international SEO. Anyone quoting a cheap package to rank in the US is quoting the content and ignoring this.

sections.h2: Why Search Console shows India impressions and almost no US ones
body: This is the question we get most often from Noida teams, usually phrased as "is our SEO broken?" Usually it isn't broken. It's honest.

You rank where you're relevant, and everything about your site says India: your links, the footer address, the rupee pricing page, the spellings, the phone format, the case studies. Results are also localised, so a team checking rankings from a Noida desk on an Indian Google account is looking at India's result set and calling it the world's.
Fix the measurement before concluding anything about the work.
numbered: **Filter Search Console by country** for every report you read. Impressions, clicks, average position and the query list all change completely.
**Set your rank tracker to the target country**, not India. A tracker configured for Delhi shows a comforting number no buyer sees.
**Segment analytics by country from day one.** Blended India-and-US figures are meaningless when conversion rates differ by an order of magnitude.
**Read the query list, not the totals.** Ten US impressions for a genuine RFP query beats four thousand Indian impressions for your company name.
**Expect the US curve to stay flat for a while.** International relevance builds as slowly as links do. If a month-two report shows a US hockey stick, ask exactly which domains linked to you.

sections.h2: Edtech admissions and IT-services RFPs are two different problems
body: Noida holds a lot of both, and the two need almost nothing in common. Retainers get wasted when an agency runs the same playbook across them.

callout.title: The seasonality point is a scheduling point
callout.body: Admission-season content published in admission season is late. Pages need to be indexed, linked and settled before the spike, which means commissioning them one to two quarters early. An agency that starts writing when your enquiries start rising has already missed the intake.

sections.h2: Sector 62, Sector 125, and the demand that really is local
body: A minority of your search demand genuinely is local, and it's worth an hour a month rather than a strategy.

Sector 62 and the Expressway sectors around 125 hold enough office density that real local queries exist — B2B services buying from neighbours, facilities and vendor searches. Google's local pack is distance-weighted, and because NCR is continuous, a Noida address also surfaces for some Delhi and Ghaziabad searchers depending on where they stand.
bullets: **A large share of "[your company] Noida" search is candidates**, not customers. It's why local traffic looks healthy while pipeline doesn't. Segment it before you celebrate it.
**A properly filled Google Business Profile is worth having anyway** — an afternoon's work, it wins your own branded searches and stops a competitor's ad sitting where your name should be.
**Don't build landing pages for NCR sectors.** "SEO for companies in Sector 62" has no meaningful demand, and thin location pages are exactly the pattern Google's scaled-content guidance targets.
**Keep the address consistent** across your site, profile and major directory listings. Costs nothing, and inconsistency quietly suppresses local visibility.

sections.h2: Rupee costs, dollar revenue, and what we actually guarantee
body: Here's the arithmetic that should change how Noida exporters think about budget. Your cost per lead is in rupees. Your deal value is in dollars or euros. That asymmetry is genuinely in your favour, and most exporters underuse it because they benchmark marketing spend against Indian competitors rather than against the acquisition cost of the market they actually sell into.

We charge ₹75,000 a month for SEO, ex-GST, with smaller sites from ₹40,000. Bundled with organic social it's ₹99,000. Convert that at today's rate and compare it to what the same scope costs an agency in your buyer's market. The comparison is usually uncomfortable in a useful direction.

The offsetting truth: paid doesn't work this way. Run [performance marketing](/performance) into the US and you pay US auction prices in dollars while earning the same dollars — the rupee advantage vanishes. Organic is where the cost asymmetry survives, which is a fair argument for weighting your mix towards it.

On the guarantee: we freeze your trailing-90-day count of qualified organic leads on day one, from your CRM, and beat it inside 90 days or keep working free until we do. Never a ranking position. And for an export-facing site we'll tell you before you sign if 90 days is the wrong window — building international link relevance from a standing start sometimes isn't a 90-day problem, and we'd rather say so than take the money.

callout.title: The honest caveat
callout.body: Beating your own baseline is easiest when the baseline is low and the site already has some authority in the target market. If you're starting from zero US relevance on a `.in` domain, expect the first 90 days to be technical and structural work, and say so out loud in the contract. See [what SEO costs in India](/cost/seo-cost-in-india) for how that changes the number.

faqs.q: Can a Noida company rank in US search results?
faqs.a: Yes, and thousands do. It needs a geographically neutral domain, correct hreflang if you run regional versions, content written the way US buyers phrase the problem, and — the expensive part — links from domains that already appear in US results. Server location is close to irrelevant if you use a CDN.

faqs.q: Why does my Search Console show mostly Indian impressions?
faqs.a: Because your links, address, pricing, spellings and case studies all say India, and because results are localised — checking rankings from a Noida desk shows you India's result set. Filter Search Console by country and set your rank tracker to the target market before drawing any conclusion.

faqs.q: Should I move from a .in domain to a .com?
faqs.a: If you're choosing today and selling abroad, choose the .com. If you already have years of equity on .in, weigh it carefully — a migration risks the traffic you have, and the honest answer depends on how much of your current organic revenue comes from India. We'd model it before recommending it.

faqs.q: How much does SEO cost for a Noida IT or edtech company?
faqs.a: Local packages advertise from around ₹10,000 a month, but international SEO is a different scope because link acquisition in a foreign market is the bulk of the cost. We start at ₹75,000/mo ex-GST, ₹40,000 for smaller sites, month-to-month after the first quarter.

faqs.q: Is local SEO worth anything for a company that exports?
faqs.a: A little. Fill in your Google Business Profile properly, keep your address consistent, and win your own branded searches — that's an afternoon of work. Beyond that, most local Noida search around your company name is job seekers rather than buyers, so don't let it inflate your reporting.

faqs.q: Do you invoice in INR or USD?
faqs.a: INR, ex-GST, with ad spend billed separately at cost and no media markup. If your revenue is in dollars, convert our fee at today's rate and compare it against agency pricing in the market you sell into rather than against Indian competitors — that's the comparison that reflects what you're actually competing for.
